examGuide.title: Mental model and derivation
examGuide.body:
Replacement is performed within the addressed set. LRU tracks recency, FIFO tracks arrival and LFU tracks a specified frequency history. Write-through updates lower memory on each write; write-back marks dirty lines and updates lower memory on eviction. Write-allocate and no-write-allocate describe write misses independently of write policy. A cold start and stated initial contents are essential for exact hit counts.

**Key relationship:** Write-back eviction traffic occurs only when the evicted valid block is dirty

examGuide.title: A repeatable solving procedure
examGuide.body:
1. Separate read/write miss handling.
2. Simulate state within each set.
3. Count dirty evictions separately from demand misses.

examGuide.title: Approach the exam question
examGuide.body: Trace block identities and set conflicts before applying LRU or write rules. Write-through updates memory on a hit; write-back marks a line dirty and writes it when evicted. Write-allocate and no-write-allocate govern misses independently of the write-hit policy. A read miss can evict a dirty block under write-back.

examGuide.title: Worked problem
examGuide.body:
A two-line fully associative LRU cache starts empty. For block references A,B,A,C,B, how many misses occur?

**Answer: 4.** A misses, B misses, A hits and becomes most recent. C misses and evicts B. The final B misses and evicts A. Total four misses. Counting distinct blocks alone would incorrectly give three.

examGuide.title: Conditions and edge cases
examGuide.body:
For a set-associative cache, LRU ordering is maintained within each set, not globally across unrelated sets.

A cache hit ratio alone does not determine memory write traffic.

examGuide.title: Worked question patterns
examGuide.body:
#### Pattern 1 · MCQ

A write-back cache normally writes a modified line to lower memory when:

- **A.** The dirty line is evicted
- **B.** A clean line is hit
- **C.** The tag is compared
- **D.** Every read occurs

**Answer: A.** A dirty eviction commits the modified block. Write-through instead propagates writes immediately.

#### Pattern 2 · MSQ

Choose true statements.

- **A.** FIFO uses insertion order
- **B.** LRU uses recent access order
- **C.** Write-allocate fetches a line on a write miss
- **D.** Write-back makes dirty bits unnecessary

**Answer: A, B, C.** Dirty bits identify modified data pending lower-memory update, so they matter for write-back.

#### Pattern 3 · NAT

An initially empty fully associative two-line LRU cache sees block sequence A,B,A,C,A. Number of misses?



**Answer: 3.** A and B miss; A hits and becomes most recent; C misses and evicts B; A hits. Total three misses.

examGuide.title: Work through the supplied PYQs
examGuide.body:
#### GATE 2024 CS1 · Q53 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/cache-policies?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Cache replacement and write policies. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. A write-back read miss can choose a dirty LRU victim, so A is false. Write-through updates memory on every write and has no dirty block awaiting write-back, proving B and disproving D.
2. A write-back write hit modifies the cached data and can change a clean block’s dirty bit from 0 to 1, proving C.
3. Select **B,C**. LRU chooses a victim but does not determine whether it needs a write-back.

#### GATE 2026 CS2 · Q52 · MSQ

[Open the original question and try it](/#/lesson/cache-policies?tab=practice)

**What is tested:** Cache replacement and write policies. Refer to the original image for complete givens and diagrams.

1. A 16-byte block means P=...B32 and R=...B36 share one block. Q=...B26 is in a different block/index. S=...6B32 differs from P by 0x1000, exactly the 4 KiB cache capacity, so it conflicts with P/R.
2. Each S evicts P/R before the next P, making every P miss. Within each round, Q does not evict P, so R always hits.
3. Q misses only initially; S misses every round after P reloads its conflicting line. Select **A,B**.
